## B.6 Type checking

`TypeCheckPhase` builds indexes for the apis and components, checks the apis, then the components (`phases/TypeCheckPhase.java:32-58`); the work is in `StaticChecker.checkCompilationUnit` (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:163`).

For an api: compound-api check, api linking, type-hierarchy acyclicity, well-formedness (`:174-220`).

For a component: `ApiTypeExtractor`, `TypeNormalizer`, a `TraitTable` and a `TypeAnalyzer`, then `Thunker` to give elided return types thunks, then `STypeChecker.typeCheck` (`:196-247`), then well-formedness again, overloading rules, export checking and the variance checker (`:268-290`).

The checker writes a type onto each expression node and produces no new representation, which is why the same `nodes/` tree continues into DESUGAR.

The variance checker is skipped when `compiled_expr_desugaring` is off, with the comment "Hack: don't run the variance checker if running the interpreter" (`StaticChecker.java:289-290`) — one of the few places in the checker that names the interpreter at all.

`Shell.getScala()` selects between the Scala checker and a Java one that no longer exists (`StaticChecker.java:228-230`); `setScala(false)` is set by `walk` (`Shell.java:422`), `typecheck-old` (`:467`), `test` (`:475`), the bare-filename arm (`:481`) and the `-typecheck-java` flag (`:865`).

== explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:365-375

## B.7 Overloading

Resolution is split between a shared rewrite and two completely different dispatch mechanisms.

The shared part: `OverloadRewriter` replaces a reference that has several candidates with a reference to a single synthetic name spelled `f{f1,f2,…}` and appends a `_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` declaring it (`compiler/OverloadRewriter.java:74-92`, `OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:110-142`).

On the interpreter path, `BuildTopLevelEnvironments.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildTopLevelEnvironments.java:128`) turns that declaration into an `OverloadedFunction`, and the actual selection happens per call, on run-time values, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787`); failure is the familiar "Failed to find any matching overload" (`:795`).

On the compiler path, `CodeGen.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6409`) hands the declaration to `OverloadSet`, which emits one dispatch method per overloaded name, testing argument types from most to least specific (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1944,1964`).

So the same phase feeds a run-time search in one world and a generated decision tree in the other, and the candidate lists they start from are different (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`): the interpreter's comes from the disambiguator, the compiler's from the type checker.

   638				 signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
   639				 isMethod: Boolean,
   640				 oa: OverloadingOracle,
   641				 debug : Boolean = false): Boolean = {
   642	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
   643	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
   644	      val b1 = fsp == gsp
   645	      val b2 = (fsp == gsp) &&
   646	      signatures.exists(third => third match {
   647	           case (ha, hsp, _) => {
   648	              val a1 = (hsp == fsp) 
   649	              val a2 = a1 && oa.lteq(ha, fa) 
   650	              val a3 = a2 && oa.lteq(ha, ga) 
   651	              val a4 = a3 && (if (isMethod && fsp.isDefined)
   652	                                oa.isMeet(withoutSelf(ha, fsp.get), withoutSelf(fa, fsp.get), withoutSelf(ga, fsp.get), false, debug)
   653	                              else oa.isMeet(ha, fa, ga, isMethod, debug))
   654	     //         if (debug)
   655	     //             println("" + ha + " " + a1 + a2 + a3 + a4)
   656	                   
   657	              a4}})
   658	      b2
   659	    }
   660	
   661	    // the self parameter of a functional method is compared as a dotted method's receiver is, wherever it sits
   662	    private def withoutSelf(a: ArrowType, i: Int): ArrowType = {
   663	      val d = a.getDomain match {
   664	        case t: TupleType =>
   665	          NF.makeTupleType(NU.getSpan(t), toJavaList(toListFromImmutable(t.getElements).zipWithIndex.filter(_._2 != i).map(_._1)))
   666	        case t => NF.makeTupleType(NU.getSpan(t), toJavaList(List[Type]()))
   667	      }
   668	      NF.makeArrowType(NU.getSpan(a), d, a.getRange, a.getInfo.getStaticParams)
   669	    }
   670	
   671	    /* The Meet Rule's closed-trait case, for functions and functional methods: the
   672	     * declarations whose domains are below both domains together hold every value of
   673	     * their overlap, as the comprises clauses show (OverloadingOracle.coversOverlap).
   674	     * For functional methods of a trait or object that provides them, the overlap is
   675	     * read without the self parameter, as meetRule reads the meet. */
   676	    private def coverageRule(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
   677	                             second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
   678	                             signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
   679	                             isMethod: Boolean,
   680	                             oa: OverloadingOracle): Boolean = {
   681	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
   682	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
   683	      if (fsp != gsp || (isMethod && fsp.isEmpty)) false
   684	      else {
   685	        val hs = signatures.collect {
   686	          case (ha, hsp, _) if hsp == fsp && !(ha eq fa) && !(ha eq ga) &&
   687	                               oa.lteq(ha, fa) && oa.lteq(ha, ga) => ha }
   688	        if (isMethod) {
   689	          val i = fsp.get
   690	          oa.coversOverlap(withoutSelf(fa, i), withoutSelf(ga, i), hs.map(withoutSelf(_, i)))
   691	        }
   692	        else oa.coversOverlap(fa, ga, hs)
   693	      }
   694	    }
   695	
   696	    /* The return types of a declaration o and of a declaration p that it keeps the type
   697	     * declaring it from inheriting (STypesUtil.providedAndOverridden). Where their parameter
   698	     * types are the same, the two are checked as the pair of an overloading was, o being the
   699	     * more specific; where o has the modifier override and widens p's, o's return type must be
   700	     * a subtype of p's (traits.tex, "Method Declarations"): with static parameters, at every
   701	     * instance of p, and where both declare as many of their own, also position by position. */
   702	    private def checkOverridingReturnType(name: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName,
   703	                                          o: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType),
   704	                                          p: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType),
   705	                                          equal: Boolean,
   706	                                          oracle: OverloadingOracle): Unit = {
   707	      def arrow(d: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType)) =
   708	        if (isFunctionalMethod(d._1)) toFunctionalMethodArrows(Set(d), oracle).headOption
   709	        else toMethodArrows(Set(d)).headOption
   710	      (arrow(o), arrow(p)) match {
   711	        case (Some(oa), Some(pa)) =>
   712	          if (equal) {
   713	            returnTypeCheck(name, oa, pa, oracle)
   714	            returnTypeCheck(name, pa, oa, oracle)
   715	          } else {
   716	            def own(a: ArrowType) = toListFromImmutable(a.getInfo.getStaticParams).filter(!_.isLifted)
   717	            // the self parameter, or a dotted method's receiver, apart
   718	            val at = oa._2.getOrElse(0)
   719	            val holds =
   720	              if (own(oa._1).isEmpty && own(pa._1).isEmpty)
   721	                isTrue(typeAnalyzer.subtype(oa._1.getRange, pa._1.getRange))(typeAnalyzer)
   722	              else oracle.sa.subtypeUA(withoutSelf(oa._1, at), withoutSelf(pa._1, at)) &&
   723	                   oracle.satisfiesPositionalRule(oa._1, pa._1)
   724	            if (!holds)
   725	              error(mergeSpan(oa._1, pa._1),
   726	                    "For " + name + ",\nthe return type of the overriding declaration " + typeAndSpanToString(oa._1) +
   727	                    " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of the declaration it overrides " + typeAndSpanToString(pa._1))
   728	          }
   729	        case _ =>
   730	      }
   731	    }
   732	
   733	    private def returnTypeCheck(name: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName,
   734	    	    			first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
   735	                                second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
   736				        oa: OverloadingOracle) = {
   737	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
   738	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
   739	//          println("Satisfies return type rule?\n   " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + "\n   " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
   740	      if (!oa.satisfiesReturnTypeRule(fa, ga)) {
   741	//        println("For " + name + ",\nthe return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
   742	        error(mergeSpan(fa, ga),
   743		      "For " + name + ",\nthe return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
   744	      }
   745	      else if (oa.lteq(fa, ga) && !oa.satisfiesPositionalRule(fa, ga))
   746	        error(mergeSpan(fa, ga),
   747	              "For " + name + ",\nthe static parameters of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should correspond position by position\n    to those of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga) +
   748	              ":\n    of the same kinds, with a return type that is a subtype of the other's under that correspondence.")
   749	    }
   750	
   751	
   752	    /* Drop the first element denoting the receiver type of the given type. */
   753	    private def dropReceiver(param: Type) = param match {
   754	      case STupleType(info, _::ty::Nil, None, Nil) => ty
   755	      case STupleType(info, elements, varargs, keywords) =>
   756	        STupleType(info, elements.takeRight(elements.size-1), varargs, keywords)
   757	      case _ => NodeFactory.makeVoidType(NU.getSpan(param))
   758	    }
   759	
   760	    def isDeclaredName(f: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName) = f match {
   761	        case SId(_,_,str) => IdentifierUtil.validId(str)
   762	        case SOp(_,_,str,_,_) => NU.validOp(str)
   763	        case _ => false
   764	    }
   765	
   766	    // the names whose declarations the overloading rules are checked for: every operator,
   767	    // symbolic ones such as + and the subscripts as well as those named by a word of
   768	    // capitals, and each identifier that isDeclaredName admits (overloading.tex,
   769	    // "Principles of Overloading"); the export check reads it too, with isDeclarationName
   770	    def isCheckedName(f: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName) = f match {
   771	        case SOp(_,_,_,_,_) => true
   772	        case _ => isDeclaredName(f)
   773	    }
   774	
   775	    def isDeclaredMethod(f: JavaFunctional) = f match {
   776	        case SDeclaredMethod(_,_) => true
   777	        case _ => false
   778	    }
   779	
   780	    def isFunction(f: JavaFunctional) = f match {
   781	        case SDeclaredFunction(_) => true
   782	        case SFunctionalMethod(_,_) => true
   783	        case SConstructor(_,_,_,_,_) => true
   784	        case _ => false
   785	    }
   786	
   787	    def isFunctionalMethod(f: JavaFunctional) = f match {
   788	        case SFunctionalMethod(_,_) => true
   789	        case _ => false
   790	    }
   791	
   792	    def isDeclaredVariable(v: JavaVariable) = v match {
   793	        case SDeclaredVariable(_) => true
   794	        case _ => false
   795	    }
   796	
   797	    private def mergeSpan(first: ArrowType, second: ArrowType): Span = mergeSpan(NU.getSpan(first), NU.getSpan(second))
   798	
   799	    private def mergeSpan(first: Span, second: Span): Span = new MultiSpan(first, second)
   800	
   801	    // whether a's declaration is written before b's: by file, then line, then column
   802	    private def writtenBefore(a: ArrowType, b: ArrowType): Boolean = {
   803	      val (x, y) = (NU.getSpan(a).getBegin(), NU.getSpan(b).getBegin())
   804	      val (fx, fy) = (String.valueOf(x.getFileName()), String.valueOf(y.getFileName()))
   805	      if (fx != fy) fx < fy
   806	      else if (x.getLine() != y.getLine()) x.getLine() < y.getLine()
   807	      else x.column() < y.column()
   808	    }
   809	
   810	    /* Returns the type of the given list of parameters. */
   811	    private def paramsToType(params: JavaList[Param], span: Span): Type =
   812	      STypesUtil.paramsToType(toListFromImmutable(params), span) match {
   813	        case Some(ty) => ty
   814	        case _ =>
   815	          val span = NU.spanAll(params)
   816	          error(span,
   817	                "Type checking couldn't infer the type of " + params)
   818	          NodeFactory.makeVoidType(span)
   819	      }
   820	
   821	    /* Returns the type of the given self type and a list of parameters. */
   822	    private def paramsToType(self: Type, params: JavaList[Param], span: Span): Type = {
   823	      val span = params.size match {
   824	        case 0 => NU.getSpan(self)
   825	        case _ => NU.spanAll(params)
   826	      }
   827	      val elems = toListFromImmutable(params).map(paramToType)
   828	      if (elems.forall(_.isDefined))
   829	        NodeFactory.makeTupleTypeOrType(span, toJavaList(List(self) ++ elems.map(_.get)))
   830	      else {
   831	        error(span,
   832	              "Type checking couldn't infer the type of " + params)
   833	        NodeFactory.makeVoidType(span)
   834	      }
   835	    }
   836	
   837	    private def error(loc: Span, msg: String) =
   838	        errors = errors ::: List(TypeError.make(msg, loc))
   839	
   840	
   841	    // The following is used by the ExportChecker.
   842	
   843	    def coverOverloading(set: Set[JavaFunction]) = {
   844	      var result = Set[JavaFunction]()
   845	      for (f <- set ; if !coveredBy(f, set)) {
   846	        result = result + f
   847	      }
   848	      result = result.filter {
   849	        case SDeclaredFunction(_) => true
   850	        case _ => false
   851	      }
   852	      result.map { case SDeclaredFunction(fd) => fd }
   853	    }
   854	
   855	    /*
   856	     * Set may contain the object f; if so, ignore it.
   857	     */
   858	    private def coveredBy(f: JavaFunction, set: Set[JavaFunction]): Boolean = {
   859	      var result = false
   860	      for (g <- set ; if !result && f != g && coveredBy(f, g)) { result = true }
   861	      result
   862	    }
   863	
   864	    /* Whether the signature of f is covered by the signature of g */
   865	    /* (If signatures are identical, then NOT covered; this is necessary for error reporting of duplicate definitions. */
   866	    private def coveredBy(f: JavaFunction, g: JavaFunction): Boolean =
   867	      globalOracle.lteq(f, g) && !globalOracle.lteq(g, f) && globalOracle.satisfiesReturnTypeRule(f, g)
   868	
   869	}

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
     2	This paper extends the work of \citet{oopsla11} with variance for
     3	polymorphic types and a dynamic dispatch algorithm.
     4	Allen et al. proposed rules for defining overloaded functions that ensure type safety
     5	under symmetric multiple dispatch in an object-oriented language with
     6	multiple inheritance, and showed how to check the rules without requiring
     7	the entire type hierarchy.
     8	They proposed the overloading rules in the context of a set of class declarations
     9	and function declarations without defining a language with complete
    10	static and dynamic semantics.  Therefore, their work does not guarantee
    11	that the static overloading rules and the way a language chooses a method
    12	to invoke at run time match correctly.
    13	% They did not provide a complete static and dynamic semantics; therefore, their work does not guarantee
    14	% that the static overloading rules and the way a language chooses a method
    15	% to invoke at run time match correctly.
    16	While FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion,
    17	and closed types in their work, they can be added in an obvious way.
    18	As the related work section of~\citet{oopsla11} discusses in detail,
    19	most earlier systems like \textit{Dubious}~\cite{dubious99,dubious02,dubious03},
    20	MultiJava~\cite{multijava06}, and F(E{\footnotesize{ML}})~\cite{FEML06} supported
    21	overloading with symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch with multiple inheritance,
    22	but without support for polymorphic methods or types.  While $\text{ML}_\le$~\cite{bm97}
    23	integrates polymorphism and symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch, it lacks
    24	multiple inheritance.
    25	
    26	ParaSail~\cite{parasail11,parasailweb} is a parallel programming language designed to support
    27	inherently safe and secure, highly parallel applications.
    28	It also constrains the scope of type parameters,
    29	prohibiting a bound on a type parameter from referring to type parameter
    30	bindings to its left, so that dynamic type inference can be fast.
    31	However, ParaSail does not support covariant and contravariant
    32	type parameters, and it does not provide any formal specification.
    33	
    34	Julia~\cite{julia15,julia17} is a dynamic programming language with symmetric
    35	multiple dispatch. It provides a type declaration and type annotation
    36	sublanguage, but does not have a static type system. Thus, it does not
    37	check the validity of overloaded methods, and only uses the
    38	subtype relation to find the most specific method among
    39	overloaded methods at run time.
    40	
    41	Various languages provide different subsets of the FGFV features.
    42	Scala~\cite{scala} supports polymorphic types
    43	with variance, but it does not support symmetric multiple dispatch.
    44	FHJ~\cite{fhj} proposed a dispatch algorithm, which uses static types at run time 
    45	to resolve overloading conflicts from unrelated methods that happen to have
    46	the same name and signature due to multiple inheritance.
    47	\citet{castagna15} presented a statically-typed calculus with dynamic
    48	(explicit) dispatch through pattern-matching, polymorphism, recursive
    49	types, semantic subtyping, and union, intersection, and negation type
    50	connectives.  Their local type inference algorithm computes sets of type
    51	substitutions to insert in appropriate places in expressions.  While
    52	their type-case expression and intersection type behave similarly to
    53	method overloading, they do not have a similar notion of overloading
    54	rules.  Since the type-case expression executes the first matching
    55	expression, it does not introduce any ambiguity.
    56	For OCaml, Garrigue~\citeyearpar{garrigue01,garrigue02} introduced a type
    57	inference system for structural polymorphism such as polymorphic records,
    58	polymorphic variants, and accurate matching.  Type constraints are
    59	described by constraint domains that are defined separately from its
    60	type system, and the constraints contain some notion of lower and upper
    61	bounds, which respectively represent required and available labels or cases.
    62	He also extended his work with CoQ mechanization \cite{garrigue10,garrigue15}.
    63	The work of Castagna and Garrigue may serve as a possible starting point
    64	for finding the necessary substitution $\sigma$ to satisfy the rule
    65	\rncite{E-Sub} for existential subtyping during static analysis.
    66	We believe that our work opens the gate to adding either variance
    67	annotation in the work of Castagna or a form of type-case in the work of
    68	Garrigue.

    41	class OverloadingOracle(implicit ta: TypeAnalyzer) extends PartialOrdering[Functional] {
    42	  
    43	  val sa = new TypeSchemaAnalyzer()
    44	  
    45	  def extend(params: List[StaticParam], where: Option[WhereClause]) = new OverloadingOracle()(ta.extend(params, where))
    46	  
    47	  override def tryCompare(x: Functional, y: Functional): Option[Int] = {
    48	    val xLEy = lteq(x,y)
    49	    val yLEx = lteq(y,x)
    50	    if (xLEy) Some(if (yLEx) 0 else -1)
    51	    else if (yLEx) Some(1) else None
    52	  }
    53	  
    54	  // Checks when f is more specific than g
    55	  def lteq(f: Functional, g: Functional): Boolean = {
    56	    (f, g) match {
    57	      case (fm: FunctionalMethod, gm: FunctionalMethod) =>
    58	        val fa = makeSpecialArrowFromFunctionalMethod(fm).get
    59	        val ga = makeSpecialArrowFromFunctionalMethod(gm).get
    60	        lteq(fa, ga)
    61	      case (_,_) =>
    62	        val fa = makeArrowFromFunctional(f, true).get
    63	        val ga = makeArrowFromFunctional(g, true).get
    64	        lteq(fa, ga)
    65	    }
    66	  }
    67	
    68	  def lteq(fa: ArrowType, ga: ArrowType): Boolean = {
    69	    val fd = sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(fa)
    70	    val gd = sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(ga)
    71	    sa.subtypeED(fd, gd)
    72	  }
    73	
    74	  def equiv(fa: ArrowType, ga: ArrowType): Boolean = lteq(fa, ga) && lteq(ga, fa)
    75	
    76	  // Checks the return type rule
    77	  def satisfiesReturnTypeRule(f: Functional, g: Functional): Boolean = {
    78	    val fa = makeArrowFromFunctional(f, true).get
    79	    val ga = makeArrowFromFunctional(g, true).get
    80	    satisfiesReturnTypeRule(fa, ga)
    81	  }
    82	
    83	  def satisfiesReturnTypeRule(x: ArrowType, y: ArrowType): Boolean =
    84	    (alphaRenameTypeSchema(x, ta.extend(toList(x.getInfo.getStaticParams), None).env),
    85	     alphaRenameTypeSchema(y, ta.extend(toList(y.getInfo.getStaticParams), None).env)) match {
    86	      case (fa@SArrowType(STypeInfo(s1, p1, sp1, w1), d1, r1, e1, i1, m1), 
    87		    ga@SArrowType(STypeInfo(s2, p2, sp2, w2), d2, r2, e2, i2, m2)) =>
    88		val fd = sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(fa)
    89		val gd = sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(ga)
    90		sa.subEDsolution(fd, gd) match {
    91		  case Some((newgd, newargs)) =>
    92		    // A static parameter of g is replaced by its solution only where the
    93		    // domains force it to equal that solution; every other one, a size the
    94		    // domains leave unsolved among them, stays g's own static parameter,
    95		    // its bound read with the forced parameters' solutions, bound in the
    96		    // special arrow beside f's, so that the rule is checked for every
    97		    // instance of g and not for one solution.
    98		    val escaped = sp2.zip(newargs).collect {
    99		      case (p, SIntArg(_, _, v: _InferenceVarInt))
   100		        if p.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindNat] || p.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindInt] => (v, p)
   101		    }
   102		    val bindEscaped: Type => Type =
   103		      if (escaped.isEmpty) (t: Type) => t
   104		      else insertNats(nSubstitution(Map(escaped.map { case (v, p) =>
   105		             (v, staticParamToArg(p).asInstanceOf[IntArg].getIntVal) }: _*)))
   106		    val forced = sp2.zip(newargs).zip(forcedArgs(fd, gd, newargs))
   107		    val str = new StaticTypeReplacer(forced.collect { case ((p, _), true) => p },
   108		                                      forced.collect { case ((_, a), true) => a })
   109		    val kept = forced.collect { case ((p, _), false) => str.replaceStaticParam(p) }
   110		    val nsp1 = sp1 ++ kept
   111		    // Build the special arrow that we use when checking the return type rule
   112		    val nta = ta.extend(nsp1, None)
   113		    val ntsa = new TypeSchemaAnalyzer()(nta)
   114		    val newr2 = bindEscaped(str.replaceIn(r2))
   115		    val ra = ntsa.normalizeUA(SArrowType(STypeInfo(s1, p1, nsp1, None), nta.meet(d1,bindEscaped(str.replaceIn(d2))), newr2, nta.mergeEffect(e1,e2), i1 && i2, None))
   116		    // Now test against that special arrow
   117		    val result = sa.subtypeUA(fa, ra)
   118		    if (!result) {
   119	// 	      println("fa = " + typeToString(fa))
   120	// 	      println("ga = " + typeToString(ga))
   121	// 	      println("ra = " + typeToString(ra))
   122	// 	      println("result = " + result + "\n")
   123		    }
   124		    result
   125		  case None => true
   126		}
   127	    }

   129	  // Which static parameters of the domain gd the relation fd <: gd forces equal to
   130	  // their solutions in newargs: the constraint of that relation, with the bounds,
   131	  // implies each such parameter's inference variable equal to its solution.  A size
   132	  // left unsolved is not forced.
   133	  private def forcedArgs(fd: Type, gd: Type, newargs: List[StaticArg]): List[Boolean] = {
   134	    val ta1 = if (getStaticParams(fd).isEmpty) ta else ta.extend(getStaticParams(fd), getWhere(fd))
   135	    val fd1 = if (getStaticParams(fd).isEmpty) fd else clearStaticParams(fd)
   136	    val nta = ta1.extend(getStaticParams(gd), getWhere(gd))
   137	    val sparams = getStaticParams(gd)
   138	    val sargs = sparams.map(makeInferenceArg)
   139	    val infTyp = staticInstantiation(sargs, gd, true, true)(ta1).getOrElse(return sparams.map(_ => true))
   140	    val c0 = nta.subtype(fd1, infTyp)
   141	    val ubs: List[CFormula] = sparams.zip(sargs).flatMap { case (p, a) => (a, staticParamBoundType(p)) match {
   142	      case (STypeArg(_, _, iv: _InferenceVarType), Some(b)) =>
   143	        staticInstantiation(sargs, insertStaticParams(b, sparams), true, true)(ta1).map(bb => upperBound(iv, bb))
   144	      case _ => None } }
   145	    val c = and(c0, and(ubs)(ta1))(ta1)
   146	    sargs.zip(newargs).map {
   147	      case (STypeArg(_, _, iv: _InferenceVarType), STypeArg(_, _, sol)) =>
   148	        implies(c, and(upperBound(iv, sol), lowerBound(iv, sol))(ta1))(ta1)
   149	      case (_, SIntArg(_, _, v: _InferenceVarInt)) => false
   150	      case _ => true
   151	    }
   152	  }
   153	
   154	  // The positional rule: when x is more specific than y and the two declare as many
   155	  // static parameters of their own, those are of the same kinds, position by position,
   156	  // and x's return type is a subtype of y's when y's own static parameters are read as
   157	  // x's, position by position, as a call that writes its static arguments hands them to
   158	  // whichever declaration of that many parameters dispatch reaches.  Declarations with
   159	  // different numbers of static parameters are not handed each other's.  The caller
   160	  // checks that x is more specific than y.
   161	  def satisfiesPositionalRule(x: ArrowType, y: ArrowType): Boolean = {
   162	    def own(a: ArrowType) = toList(a.getInfo.getStaticParams).filter(!_.isLifted)
   163	    val (xo, yo) = (own(x), own(y))
   164	    if (xo.isEmpty || xo.size != yo.size) return true
   165	    if (xo.zip(yo).exists { case (p, q) => p.getKind.getClass != q.getKind.getClass }) return false
   166	    (alphaRenameTypeSchema(x, ta.extend(toList(x.getInfo.getStaticParams), None).env),
   167	     alphaRenameTypeSchema(y, ta.extend(toList(y.getInfo.getStaticParams), None).env)) match {
   168	      case (SArrowType(STypeInfo(_, _, sp1, _), _, r1, _, _, _),
   169	            SArrowType(STypeInfo(_, _, sp2, _), _, r2, _, _, _)) =>
   170	        val nta = ta.extend(sp1 ++ sp2.filter(_.isLifted), None)
   171	        val str = new StaticTypeReplacer(sp2.filter(!_.isLifted),
   172	                                          sp1.filter(!_.isLifted).map(p => staticParamToArg(p)))
   173	        isTrue(nta.subtype(r1, str.replaceIn(r2)))(nta)
   174	    }
   175	  }
   176	
   177	  // The Meet Rule's closed-trait case, for fa and ga without static parameters, whose
   178	  // domains overlap and neither of which is below the other: the declarations hs, each
   179	  // below both, together hold every value of the overlap.  The overlap is cut by the
   180	  // comprises clauses of the closed traits in it, a trait read as the union of its
   181	  // listed types; a part two of whose types exclude is empty; every other part must be
   182	  // below the domain of one of hs.  What it cannot show is not covered: a part with no
   183	  // closed trait left to cut, a cut that repeats a part on its own path, and a search
   184	  // longer than coverageCuts cuts.  A local judgement of overload checking: its result
   185	  // is never a subtyping fact.
   186	  private val coverageCuts = 1000
   187	
   188	  def coversOverlap(fa: ArrowType, ga: ArrowType, hs: List[ArrowType]): Boolean = {
   189	    def ground(a: ArrowType) = getStaticParams(a).isEmpty
   190	    if (hs.isEmpty || !ground(fa) || !ground(ga) || !hs.forall(ground)) return false
   191	    def positions(d: Type): Option[List[Type]] = d match {
   192	      case STupleType(_, es, None, Nil) => Some(es)
   193	      case _: TupleType => None
   194	      case t => Some(List(t))
   195	    }
   196	    type Part = List[List[Type]]
   197	    def canon(cs: List[Type]): List[Type] = cs.distinct.sortBy(_.toString)
   198	    def conj(cs: List[Type]): Type = makeMaybeIntersectionType(toJavaList(cs))
   199	    def asType(p: Part): Type = p match {
   200	      case List(cs) => conj(cs)
   201	      case _ => makeTupleType(toJavaList(p.map(conj)))
   202	    }
   203	    def empty(p: Part) = p.exists(cs => cs.exists(a => cs.exists(b => !(a eq b) && ta.definitelyExcludes(a, b))))
   204	    val hds = hs.map(sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow)
   205	    def covered(p: Part) = { val t = asType(p); hds.exists(h => ta.lteq(t, h)) }
   206	    // A closed trait's listed types, its static arguments substituted; a functional
   207	    // method's self type is read as its trait.
   208	    def listed(t: Type): Option[List[Type]] = t match {
   209	      case tt: TraitType => ta.typeCons(tt.getName) match {
   210	        case ti: ProperTraitIndex if !ti.comprisesTypes.isEmpty && !NU.isComprisesEllipses(ti.ast) =>
   211	          val cs = ta.comprisesClause(tt)
   212	          if (cs.size != ti.comprisesTypes.size) None else Some(canon(cs.toList))
   213	        case _ => None
   214	      }
   215	      case ts: TraitSelfType => listed(ts.getNamed)
   216	      case _ => None
   217	    }
   218	    (positions(sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(fa)), positions(sa.makeDomainWithSelfFromArrow(ga))) match {
   219	      case (Some(fs), Some(gs)) if fs.size == gs.size =>
   220	        var cuts = 0
   221	        var work: List[(Part, Set[Part])] = List((fs.zip(gs).map { case (a, b) => canon(List(a, b)) }, Set[Part]()))
   222	        while (!work.isEmpty) {
   223	          val (p, path) = work.head
   224	          work = work.tail
   225	          if (!empty(p) && !covered(p)) {
   226	            val cut = p.indices.view.flatMap(i => p(i).view.flatMap(c => listed(c).map(ls => (i, c, ls)))).headOption
   227	            cut match {
   228	              case None => return false
   229	              case Some((i, c, ls)) =>
   230	                cuts += 1
   231	                if (cuts > coverageCuts || path.contains(p)) return false
   232	                work = ls.map(l => (p.updated(i, canon(p(i).filter(_ != c) :+ l)), path + p)) ++ work
   233	            }
   234	          }
   235	        }
   236	        true
   237	      case _ => false
   238	    }
   239	  }

usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does
                             not block it; a row keeps its own cells

facts-extract: part 1 of 1. Its 1 part prints 2278 bytes, about 1000 tokens.
Asked for, and where it is:
  "exclusion fork"                                           F-45, by a former title  [1952 bytes]

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:40
F-45 was retitled: its former title "The exclusion fork, priced three ways and dated" holds the words; its title now is "Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch."
- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".

content.content:
/**
 * @param decl A declaration appearing within a trait declaration
 * @param traitStaticParameters
 * @return
 * For each functional declaration (getters, setters, methods, functional methods) we verify 
 * the correct polarity of the trait's type parameters for 
 * 1. The return type
 * 2. The domain type
 * 3. The static parameters of the functional declaration
 * 
 * For now, we do not handle abstract variable declaration. Need to check whether they are incolved
 * in variance clauses.
 */
private def verifyTraitDeclaration(decl: Decl, traitStaticParameters: List[StaticParam]): Boolean = {

       decl match {
         
         case m: FnDecl =>
           val rangeType = m.getHeader().getReturnType().unwrap()
           val domainParams = scalaify(m.getHeader().getParams()).asInstanceOf[List[Param]]
           // a varargs parameter's arguments are its element type, in the domain's position
           val domainTypes = domainParams map (p => (if (p.getVarargsType().isSome()) p.getVarargsType()
                                                     else p.getIdType()).unwrap().asInstanceOf[Type])
           val staticParams = scalaify(m.getHeader().getStaticParams()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticParam]]
           // First, analyze the arrow type range
           verifyType(rangeType,1)(traitStaticParameters) &&  
           // Second, analyze the arrow type domain
           scan(domainTypes, { verifyType(_:Type,-1)(traitStaticParameters) }) &&
           // Third, analyze the arrow type parameters
           scan(staticParams, { verifyFunDeclStaticParam(_:StaticParam,-1)(traitStaticParameters) })
         
         case v: VarDecl => 
           val lvalues = scalaify(v.getLhs()).asInstanceOf[List[LValue]]
           scan(lvalues, { verifyVarDecl(_:LValue)(traitStaticParameters) } )

         case _ => 
           error("Variance checker: Unknown form of declaration: " + decl,decl)
           false
       
       }

 }

 private def verifyVarDecl(v: LValue)(implicit traitStaticParameters:List[StaticParam]): Boolean = {
   
   val hidden = v.getMods().isHidden()
   val settable = v.getMods().isSettable()
   val typ = v.getIdType().unwrap()    // John: for now, I'm assuming that abstract field declarations always have a type  

   val pol = (hidden,settable) match {
     case (true,true) => -1
     case (true,false) => 1 // This one is actually ruled out by the parser
     case (false,false) => 1
     case (false,true) => 0 
   }
   
   verifyType(typ.asInstanceOf[Type],pol)  
   
 }

 private def flip(polarity: Int) = polarity * -1

/**
 * @param s
 * @return
 */
private def verifyFunDeclStaticParam(s: StaticParam, polarity: Int)(implicit traitStaticParameters:List[StaticParam]): Boolean = {
   
		 scan(traitStaticParameters, { verifyParam(_:StaticParam,s.getName().getText(),polarity,s) })	&&
		 scan(scalaify(s.getExtendsClause()).asInstanceOf[List[Type]], { verifyType(_: Type,polarity) } ) &&
		 scan(scalaify(s.getDominatesClause()).asInstanceOf[List[Type]], { verifyType(_: Type,flip(polarity)) })
   
 } 	
 
 /**
 * @param ty The type to analyze
 * @param polarity The current polarity  
 * @param traitStaticParameters The type parameters from the trait being declared
 * @return
 */
private def verifyType(ty: Type, polarity: Int)(implicit traitStaticParameters:List[StaticParam]): Boolean = {

   ty match {

     case t: VarType =>
       scan(traitStaticParameters, { verifyParam(_: StaticParam,t.getName().getText(),polarity,ty) })

     case t: TraitType =>
       val traitParams = scalaify(t.getTraitStaticParams()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticParam]]
       val traitArgs = scalaify(t.getArgs()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticArg]]
       val traitInfo = traitParams.zip(traitArgs)
       val filteredTraitInfo = traitInfo filter (_._1.getKind().equals(new KindType()))
       (true /: filteredTraitInfo) ((b, x) => b && verifyType(x._2.asInstanceOf[Type],x._1.getVariance() * polarity))

     case ts: TraitSelfType => 
       val t: TraitType = ts.asInstanceOf[TraitSelfType].getNamed().asInstanceOf[TraitType]
       val traitParams = scalaify(t.getTraitStaticParams()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticParam]]
       val traitArgs = scalaify(t.getArgs()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticArg]]
       val traitInfo = traitParams.zip(traitArgs)
       val filteredTraitInfo = traitInfo filter (_._1.getKind().equals(new KindType()))
       (true /: filteredTraitInfo) ((b, x) => b && verifyType(x._2.asInstanceOf[Type],x._1.getVariance() * polarity))
       
     case t: ArrowType =>
       verifyType(t.getDomain(),flip(polarity)) && verifyType(t.getRange(),polarity)

     /*
      * The following compound types (tuple, intersection, union) are simple:
      * recursively verify their constituents, with same polarity. 
      */
       
     case t: TupleType =>
       val types = scalaify(t.getElements()).asInstanceOf[List[Type]]
       scan(types, { verifyType(_: Type,polarity) })
       
     case t: IntersectionType =>
       val types = scalaify(t.getElements()).asInstanceOf[List[Type]]
       scan(types, { verifyType(_: Type,polarity) })

     case t: UnionType =>
        val types = scalaify(t.getElements()).asInstanceOf[List[Type]]
        scan(types, { verifyType(_: Type,polarity) })

     case t: AnyType => true

     case t: BottomType => true

     case t =>
       error("Variance checker: Unknown form of type: " + t,t)
       false

   }

 }

content.content:
Formalised by the team in Welterweight
   Fortress (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:48-49`, "Type parameters of traits can be
   covariant, contravariant, or invariant", `paper.tick:556`), with the rule generalised as the
   **Ancestors Meet Rule**: a trait may extend two instances of one trait only if it also extends
   an instance below both (`static.tick:83-89`). Naden's write-up of 2012-08-31 (`8015b17f4`,
   `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:499-566`) adopts the same: "Fortress supports
   variant generic types", covariant multiple instantiation exclusion, plus a restriction on
   crossed instantiations.
3. **A lower bound on a method's parameter**, the companion of a covariant container's methods:
   `f[\U dominates T\](x: U): U` (`compiler_tests/VarianceTest4.fss:16`, Welterweight's lower
   bounds, `grammar.tick:44-47`). **[read]**
4. **A generic coercion between instantiations**, the specification's own spelling:
   `coerce[\S extends Number\](x: Vector[\S\]) where {T widens or coerces S}`
   (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:213-216`). **[read]**
   - **Refused on both paths [measured, `AltCovariantCoerce`].**
   - The compiled checker reports `Cyclic type hierarchy: Type C transitively extends/coerces to
     itself.` Its acyclicity check records a coercion's source by trait name only, dropping the
     static arguments (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:102-121`). So `C[\T\]`'s coercion from
     `C[\S\]` reads as `C` coercing from `C`. **[read]**

# The POPL 2019 examples, sorted for the test suite

## In short

- The paper and the talk hold 24 worked examples once the talk's builds that repeat a paper example are folded into it: 11 in group A, 4 in group B, 9 in group C.
- Of the 11 in group A, today's tree fails 5: four on one path, and one (A8) on both, which its gated expected failures already record. Two tests derived from group B and C examples fail too:
  - walk loads an object that inherits `m(x: Number)` with a body from two unrelated traits (p. 11:2; row 444's family);
  - walk loads `f(x: B): C` beside `f(x: C): B` with `object C extends B`, the talk's "NOT TYPE-SOUND" set (slide 4; a new row);
  - walk loads two generic `sort`s bounded by `A` and by `B` with no declaration at their meet (p. 11:5, slide 7; row 373);
  - the compiled path refuses the talk's opening `add` set, because the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` is an open trait (slide 2; a new row);
  - the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple fails on both paths, as its gated expected failures say (p. 11:13; rows 537 and 539);
  - derived: the paper's `sort` set with its meet written `P extends { A, B }` dies compiled (row 537), and the invariant core of the paper's `sort`/`merge` example fails on both paths (p. 11:7; one new compiled row, one walk row optional).
- Group B holds no new question for Pavol. The paper's two sets that rest on "C is the only subtype of both A and B" become valid in Fortress through `comprises` clauses, which the revival's Meet Rule reads as coverage; the union instance of `O.m(3, true)` is his decision for the bound; the No Duplicates wording is row 696.
- Group C waits on the `covariant` keyword (row 404), lower bounds on a method's type parameters, and the static return type carried to run time (phase 5).

## How the examples were run

- Each Fortress form is a test program in the form the `fortress-repo` skill gives (`tests-writing.md`, "A test program"): `component Name`, `export Executable`, the declarations shown, and `run(): () = do ... end` with the body shown. The scratch copies live in the tree's ignored `tmp/` and are not committed.
- Under walk: `bin/fortress walk P.fss`. Compiled: `bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`. Both with `FORTRESS_CACHES` pointing at a private copy of `default_repository/caches`, so the shared caches took no scratch entry.
- The existing tests named below were run through the harness: `harness-one.sh` on `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss` and `XXXGenericBesidePlainSameDomain.fss` printed `OK (2 tests)`; `junit.sh` with `ONE_JVM=1` on `OverloadExistentialMeetLink.test`, `XXXOverloadExistentialMeet.test`, `XXX2f.test`, `GenericInstanceUnfixedLink.test` and `XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed.test` printed `OK (5 tests)`, each `XXX` file as "Saw expected failure".
- In FGFV a method is called `e.m(e')`; the Fortress forms use top-level functions, which the revival overloads by the same rules (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). FGFV's classes become traits, or objects where the example needs a value.
- An overloading that breaks a rule is a static error on both paths: the rules are "checked statically" for the declarations, "whether or not these calls actually appear" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). Walk checks overload sets when it loads a program (`fortress-repo` skill, `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), so its form of a static error is a refusal at load.

## Group A: rules the revival implements

### A1. Two traits each give `m(x: Number)` a body; an object extends both (p. 11:2)

- **Source.** §1: classes `A` and `B` each declare `m` at `Number`, `C` extends both, and `c.m(0)` is ambiguous, "because neither A nor B is more specific than each other".

- **Test.** None new.

### A8. The `ArrayList`/`List` triple (p. 11:13)

- **Source.** §4.2: `m[P](x: ArrayList[P])`, `m[Q <: T](y: List[Q])`, `m[R <: T](z: ArrayList[R])`, with `ArrayList` below `List` and both invariant. The set is valid, though the domains' intersection is not a subtype of the third's domain; existential reduction closes the gap by instantiation exclusion.
- **Fortress form.** The tree's `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadExistentialMeet.fss` and `tests/XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss`, in the names `Seq`, `ArraySeq` and `Num`.
- **Expected.** Valid on both paths; an array of numbers runs the third, an array of strings the first (`advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters": exclusion "by existential reduction").
- **Today.** Both fail, as gated. Walk refuses at load (row 539, "OK Saw expected exception"); the compiled run dies, "Unable to read serialized data for XXXOverloadExistentialMeet?$\=m{...}" (row 537).
- **Test.** Exists on both paths. Nothing new.

### A9. Inference from an invariant position (pp. 11:24-25)

- **Source.** §5.4: a `List[String]` passed to `foo[T](x: List[T])` binds `T` to `String`, the cheap invariant case of run-time inference.
- **Fortress form.**

      object Lst[\T\] end
      object Tag[\T\] end
      foo[\T\](x: Lst[\T\]): Tag[\T\] = Tag[\T\]
      same[\T\](a: Tag[\T\], b: Tag[\T\]): String = "same"
      run body: assert(same(foo(Lst[\String\]), Tag[\String\]), "same", "T is String")

- **Expected.** `T` is `String` (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`, "The Static Arguments of a Call", the first item of "Instantiation").
- **Today.** Both paths print `PASS`.
- **Existing tests.** The shape is inside many tests, for example `compiler_tests/InferUnionInstanceArg.fss` (`one[\T\](a: BoxT[\T\])`) and `compiler_tests/DispatchRenamedArmRungG.fss`.
- **Test.** None new.

### B3. `O.m(3, true)` annotated at the union `Int ⊔ Boolean` (p. 11:21)

- **Source.** §5.2.5: `object O' [Q] m'(x: Q): Q`, `object O m[P](x: P, y: P): P = O'[P].m'(x)`, and the typed call `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`; at run time the dispatcher infers `P` as the union, and the union then flows into `m'`.
- **What departs.** The revival's static inference gives such a parameter its bound, "the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, Any if it has none", never the union (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`, "The Static Arguments of a Call", with its `revival-inference` callout; POSITIONS, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`": "never the union of the arguments' types"). The paper gives no static inference algorithm (p. 11:25), and its dispatcher, given the static type `Any`, would take `Any` too; so the departure is from the paper's example, not from its rules.
- **Fortress form.** `object Op[\Q extends Any\] end`, `m[\P extends Any\](x: P, y: P): Op[\P\] = Op[\P\]`, and `kind(m(3, true))` by a `typecase` over `Op[\Any\]` and `Op[\Object\]`.
- **Today.** Both paths print `PASS`: `P` is `Any`. Written as the paper writes it, with no bound, walk prints `PASS` and the compiled checker refuses `Op[\Any\]`, "The static argument Any does not satisfy the corresponding bound Object" (row 412, the compiled path's implicit bound `Object`).
- **Ledger and questions.** None: decided. `compiler_tests/InferLoneUnbounded.fss` and `tests/InferLoneUnboundedWalk.fss` gate the bound (row 516, fixed).

### B4. The No Duplicates Rule (Fig. 5, p. 11:13; slide 12)

- **Source.** A rule with no worked example: [No-Dup-Not-Less] and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domains are each below the other. The `sort` and `ArrayList` sets meet it "trivially" (p. 11:6).
- **What departs.** The revival's text states the rule on a strict "more specific", so it refuses nothing, and an equivalent pair falls to the Meet Rule (row 696, `advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters").
- **Fortress form.** `object Box[\T\] end`, `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\]): ZZ32 = 1` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\]): ZZ32 = 2`, called on `Box[\String\]`.
- **Today.** Compiled: refused by the checker's own duplicate check, "There are multiple declarations of dup with the same parameter type: Box[\T\]". Walk: loads and prints `1`, row 373's family.
- **Ledger.** A note on row 696: the checker already refuses the pair, so only the text is wrong; walk runs it.

## Group C: features the revival lacks

| # | Source | The example | Feature it needs | Ledger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | p. 11:3 | Scala's `List[+A]` with `:::[B >: A](prefix: List[B]): List[B]` | a covariant class parameter; a lower bound on a method's type parameter (Fortress writes it as a `where` clause, `where { A extends B }`) | row 404; row 677 (the compiled checker reads no `where` constraint as a bound); the code generator refuses a `where` clause (`fortress-repo` skill, `compiler.md`) |
| C2 | p. 11:6; slide 9 | covariant `ListC` and `SortedListC`: `sort(ListC[A])`, `sort(ListC[B])` overlap at `ListC[C]`; `sort(ListC[C]): SortedListC[C]` disambiguates | `covariant` | row 404 |
| C3 | p. 11:6; slide 9 | the same with `SortedListI` invariant: `SortedListI[A]` is not above `SortedListI[C]`, so the set breaks the Return Type Rule ("NOT TYPE-SOUND!") | `covariant` | row 404 |
| C4 | p. 11:7; slides 9 and 16 | `sort[P](x: ListC[C]): SortedListI[P]` beside the two plain `sort`s, and `merge[P]` of two `SortedListI[P]`; run time must take `P = A` from the static type | `covariant`; the static return type at run time on the compiled path | row 404; PLAN phase 5 (`OverloadSet.java:2048`); its invariant core is A-C4 |
| C5 | p. 11:9; slide 8 | `trait T[+P, -Q, =S]` with `U2 <: U1`: `T[U2, U1, U1] <: T[U1, U2, U1]` | `covariant`, `contravariant` | row 404; row 17 (the specification's `where`-clause covariance idiom refused) |
| C6 | p. 11:12 | the type context of `((P, T[Q]) → Any)` with `T` contravariant: `P` must be contravariant or invariant, `Q` covariant or invariant | the variance position check of [D-Method] | row 404 |
| C7 | p. 11:19 | the Cartesian product of bound lists, `⟨A ⊔ E, B ⊔ F⟩, ...`, from matching a union | union and intersection types at run time, and the paper's match-and-solve dispatcher | none; phase 5 |
| C8 | pp. 11:20-21 | `append[P, {P} <: Q]` over covariant `SortedList` and `List`; static type `List[C3]`, ilks `SortedCons[C1]` and `Cons[C2]`; the first fails to match, the second runs at `[C3/P, C3/Q]`, with the match and solve derivations | `covariant`; a lower bound on a method's type parameter; the static return type at run time | rows 404 and 677; phase 5 |
| C9 | p. 11:24 | the Ancestor Meet Rule's equivalences `T[α ⊓ α'] ≡ T[α] ⊓ T[α']` for covariant `T`, `T[α ⊔ α'] ≡ T[α] ⊓ T[α']` for contravariant `T`, and only `(T[α] ⊔ T[α']) <: T[α ⊔ α']` | `covariant`, `contravariant`, and union and intersection types | row 404 |

All nine wait on worklist item 12 and on POSITIONS, "The `covariant` keyword is future work". None needs a row now beyond those named.

An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.  Therefore, such an operator method
declaration must satisfy the overloading rules
with every operator declaration in the same component.



In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter whose type is
a naked type parameter declared with the bound \TYP{Any} written, as
\EXP{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, cannot be
overloaded.  This restriction prevents ambiguous overloadings such as
the following:
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T): Set[\T\]
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T, y: T): Set[\T\]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T, y\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
\end{Fortress}
The type parameter of \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}} may be instantiated with
\TYP{(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z})} or \TYP{\mathbb{Z}}.  If this is the
case then the call \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}(3, 4)}, where 3 and 4 have type
\TYP{\mathbb{Z}}, is ambiguous.
A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, whose bound is
\TYP{Any} as well (\secref{type-param}), does not fall under this restriction:
\library\ declare the factory
\EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()}.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 stated this
restriction for a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} while a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause was bounded by \TYP{Object}
(\secref{type-param}).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any} it would forbid overloading every functional
whose single parameter's type is such a type parameter, the factory above among
them.
The restriction is stated as the compiled type checker applies it, to a bound
written \TYP{Any}; the checker draws no such refusal on \library.}

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:25
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:43
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.

POSITIONS.md:46
- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.

POSITIONS.md:48
- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. If none of the compiled checker's attempts at the call accepts `f(g(x))` (P-49 gives the order of those attempts), the checker checks `g(x)` again, once for each declaration of `f`, with that declaration's parameter type at `g(x)`'s position as its expected type. The retry covers every inner call with inferred static arguments, not only one whose type parameter occurs in its result type alone. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. The declaration whose retry succeeds is kept, or the most specific of several; otherwise the call goes on as it would without the retry. The measurement behind the decision is in `explorations/reviews/argument-context-probe.md`.

POSITIONS.md:56
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:81
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
